titre: The 1948 Freedom of Association Convention Never Says the Word Strike
accroche: In 1948, the ILO adopts a text on freedom of association that never utters the word strike. It would take seventy-eight years to settle the question.
contenu_vulgarise:
On July 9, 1948, the International Labour Conference adopts, in San Francisco, Convention No. 87 on freedom of association and protection of the right to organise. It enters into force on July 4, 1950, and becomes one of the International Labour Organization's so-called fundamental conventions. Its Article 2 states that workers and employers, without distinction whatsoever, have the right, without previous authorization, to establish organizations of their own choosing. Its Article 3 guarantees them the right to draw up their own constitutions and rules, elect their representatives, and organize their administration and activities.

## A Word Missing from the Text

The word strike appears nowhere in these articles, nor in the 1948 preparatory work. The drafters debate the question and choose not to include it. For decades, two of the ILO's supervisory bodies, the Committee on Freedom of Association and the Committee of Experts, nonetheless infer that the right to strike is an inseparable corollary of the freedom of association protected by the convention. They base this reasoning on the same Articles 2 and 3: for a union, organizing its activities and formulating its programs includes the possibility of stopping work.

## The 2012 Rupture

In June 2012, the employers' group at the International Labour Conference refuses, for the first time, to let the committee responsible for supervising the application of conventions examine cases related to the right to strike. Its argument: no provision of Convention No. 87, read in its ordinary sense, implies a right to strike, and the preparatory work shows its drafters did not intend to include one. The deadlock paralyzes part of the ILO's supervisory machinery for several years, with neither side backing down.

## An International Court to Settle a Silence

On November 10, 2023, the ILO's Governing Body, noting a deep and persistent disagreement among its three groups, refers a request for an advisory opinion to the International Court of Justice for the first time since the Court's creation in 1945, under Article 37 of its Constitution — only the second time it is called on to interpret an international labour convention. Eighteen states and five international organizations are heard during the hearings of October 2025. On May 21, 2026, the Court responds by ten votes to four: the right to strike of workers and their organizations is indeed protected by Convention No. 87. It specifies, however, that it is not ruling on its content, its scope, or the conditions for its exercise.

A text can therefore ground a right for seventy-eight years without ever stating it, through the sheer repeated reading given to it by its supervisory bodies, until a disagreement becomes too costly to remain implicit. What the convention actually protects remains, after the 2026 opinion, almost entirely to be written.

repere.texte: On May 21, 2026, the International Court of Justice rules by ten votes to four. It is the first time the ILO has brought a case before the Court since its creation in 1945, and only the second time the Court has interpreted an international labour convention.
repere.source: International Labour Organization, press release of May 21, 2026

quiz.question: Why did the International Court of Justice have to rule, in 2026, on ILO Convention No. 87?
choix: Because a state had explicitly refused to apply the convention on its territory
Because the 1948 text never mentions strikes, and a right had been inferred from it without the employers' agreement
Because the convention had been amended in 2012 without the unions' agreement
Because the United States was demanding to be bound by a convention it had not ratified
quiz.explication: The 1948 text never says "strike": it was the ILO's supervisory bodies that inferred this right, which the employers contested starting in 2012. The convention was never amended, no state denounced it, and the United States was only authorized to take part in the proceedings before the Court, without being bound by it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In what year was ILO Convention No. 87 adopted?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry notes that the convention was adopted on July 9, 1948, in San Francisco, at the 31st session of the International Labour Conference.

quiz_supplementaire.question: By how many votes did the International Court of Justice rule, on May 21, 2026, that the right to strike is protected by Convention No. 87?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry specifies that the Court ruled by ten votes to four, without settling the content or scope of the right.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What triggers the deadlock at the International Labour Conference in June 2012?
choix: The employers' group's refusal to let cases related to the right to strike be examined
The resignation of the ILO's Director-General
A general strike by ILO staff in Geneva
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry notes that the employers' group refuses, for the first time, to let the supervisory committee examine cases related to the right to strike, arguing that the text does not imply one.
